title: Custom Exception Classes
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of custom exception classes in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply custom exception classes in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to organizing exception hierarchies and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Custom Exception Classes through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding custom exception classes helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Custom Exception Classes helps you reason about defining application exceptions. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Defining application exceptions. Then connect it to Exception messages and context. The remaining syllabus points—Organizing exception hierarchies—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Example: Custom Exception Classes
content_blocks.code:
class InvalidScore < StandardError; end
begin
  raise InvalidScore, "score out of range"
rescue InvalidScore => error
  puts error.message
end

items.title: Assuming the happy path is enough
items.text: Test an empty value, a boundary value, and one invalid value before depending on the behavior.

items.title: Treating an example as a universal rule
items.text: Check Ruby version, runtime implementation, and third-party library documentation when behavior is version-sensitive.

items.title: Mixing too many concerns
items.text: Separate input parsing, domain behavior, and output so each piece is easier to test.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports custom exception classes. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for custom exception classes using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Organizing exception hierarchies), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Recap
